# Why does my RPM drop when sitting idle at traffic lights?

When you shift a manual transmission into neutral while stopped, you are fundamentally changing how your engine management system calculates load and target speed. In this scenario, the engine is no longer supporting the vehicle's inertia or overcoming drivetrain drag; it is effectively running in "open loop" regarding torque demand until the throttle position sensor (TPS) dictates otherwise. The behavior you describe—a rapid dip to 500 RPM followed by a spike to 1200 and then a slow return to baseline—is almost certainly the Idle Air Control System (IACS) or its modern electronic equivalent hunting for an equilibrium point.

In older mechanical systems, this was handled by a vacuum-operated valve that adjusted airflow based on throttle position. Modern vehicles rely on an Electronic Throttle Body (ETB), often referred to as drive-by-wire technology. The Engine Control Unit (ECU) continuously monitors the Mass Airflow Sensor (MAF) and calculates the exact amount of air entering the intake manifold. At idle, particularly in neutral, there is no load from the transmission. However, the ECU must account for parasitic loads like the alternator, water pump, and air conditioning compressor.

The specific oscillation you are seeing—dropping to 500 RPM and correcting to 1200—is a classic sign of an adaptive idle control loop reacting to transient airflow disturbances or sensor noise. When the ECU detects the RPM falling below its target threshold (let's say 800 RPM), it commands the throttle plate to open slightly wider, injecting more air to raise the speed. If the correction overshoots the target due to a slight lag in the actuator response time, the RPM spikes to 1200. The ECU then closes the throttle, causing the drop back down, and the cycle repeats until it stabilizes at your baseline of 1000 RPM. This happens about three times a minute because the system is likely struggling against minor variables such as intake vacuum leaks, clogged idle air passages, or a dirty Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) sending erratic voltage signals to the ECU.

From an implementation standpoint, this behavior can be diagnosed by inspecting the throttle body. Over time, carbon buildup accumulates on the throttle plate and the IAC valve ports, restricting airflow when the ECU tries to command low-RPM operation. If you attempt to clean these passages, you may need to perform a throttle relearn procedure so the ECU recalibrates its baseline map. In many vehicles, this involves turning the ignition key to the "on" position without starting the engine for 10 seconds, then waiting 20 seconds before cranking. The ECU will initialize default values and re-learn the idle characteristics over the next few minutes of operation.

Another potential culprit is the MAF sensor. If it reports slightly higher airflow than reality at low speeds, the ECU injects too much fuel, but in a neutral idle scenario where throttle modulation is precise, even small discrepancies can cause instability. Conversely, a vacuum leak downstream of the throttle body introduces unmetered air. The ECU compensates by retarding ignition timing or enriching the mixture to cool the cylinder head, which increases exhaust pressure and causes that momentary RPM dip before the system corrects itself.

While this specific oscillation pattern is often benign if the engine eventually stabilizes at 1000 RPM, persistent hunting indicates a component that needs attention. If the idle drops below 400 RPM or stalls repeatedly during these cycles, it suggests the corrective action from the ECU cannot overcome the airflow restriction or leak fast enough. In such cases, replacing the IAC valve or cleaning the throttle body is usually the first line of defense before considering more invasive diagnostics like checking fuel pressure or ignition timing synchronization.
